notes:
I've put together notes on most of Proverbs 4, but there are gaps. My tools stopped working early, so I couldn't read several of the sources you listed: netbible.org (I only saw NET notes quoted on preceptaustin), bibleodyssey.org, oca.org, gotquestions.org, or any Methodist or Pentecostal site. Verses 24–27 have the least material.

**Chapter overview**
- The chapter falls into three parts: getting wisdom (vv. 1–13), avoiding the wicked (vv. 14–19), and a closing summary of practical faith (vv. 20–27). IN this chapter, Solomon renews his exhortations to us to get wisdom, ver. 1–13, and to avoid temptations, ver. 14–19. The chapter concludes with a short sum of practical religion. (Lawson) https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-4-commentary
- The Pulpit Commentary says the key idea is "instruction," meaning discipline (Hebrew *musar*). It also notes that Melanchthon read the chapter as a call to obedience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/4-1.htm

**v. 1:** Guzik thinks the double call to "hear" and "pay attention" suggests the children may resist. Parents should keep teaching even when that happens. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/ Preceptaustin says "hear" means paying attention and also obeying. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-4-commentary

**v. 2:** The father is confident his teaching is good because it rests on Scripture. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/ The word for "directive" is *torah*, which ties David's words to God's Word. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-4-commentary
- *Catholic/patristic:* The early church writer Hippolytus notes that the law is called a good gift, and that a person "forsakes" the law by breaking it. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0502.htm

**v. 3:** Waltke (via Guzik) reads "a son to my father" as a *true* son in the moral and spiritual sense. On "only child": Bathsheba had other sons, but Solomon was her special son and God's chosen heir. Waltke compares Isaac being called Abraham's "only" son. Trapp adds that Solomon's later fall was more to blame because he had been raised so carefully. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/ Jensen sees Solomon fondly recalling both David and Bathsheba. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-4-commentary

**v. 4:** Benson and Poole say David is quoted at least up to verse 10. They take "and live" as a promise phrased as a command. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/4-4.htm The Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) has "they taught me," as if David and Bathsheba taught together. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/4-4.htm Matthew Henry says words that are not hidden in the heart will not be kept. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-4-commentary
- *Commentators differ on "live":* The Pulpit Commentary says it means a long, happy *earthly* life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/4-4.htm Matthew Henry instead speaks of eternal death and eternal life being at stake. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_004.cfm

**v. 5:** "Get" (*qanah*) means to buy, so wisdom costs something (Waltke, Wiersbe). Kidner says what it takes is decision, not brains. Guzik notes the irony that Solomon later turned away himself (1 Kings 11). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/ The Pulpit Commentary pictures the father urging wisdom on his son like a merchant pressing his goods. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-4.html

**v. 6:** Ross notes the feminine verbs. Wisdom is pictured as a bride and also as a powerful patron who protects. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/ McGee quotes Pascal: divine knowledge must be loved before it can be understood. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-4-commentary Benson says doing good is not enough without sincerely loving it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/4-4.htm

**v. 7:** The Pulpit Commentary reports two ways of translating this. One is "the beginning of wisdom is: get wisdom." The other, which it prefers, is the familiar "wisdom is the principal thing." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-4.html Preceptaustin notes that repeating "acquire" shows wisdom is a lifelong process, not a one-time decision. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-4-commentary
- *Catholic:* Haydock's Catholic commentary, citing Augustine, says the first step of wisdom is to want it; it is "the one thing necessary." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/proverbs-4.html

**v. 8:** Kitchen: if you lift wisdom up, it lifts you with it; if you try to lift yourself up, you will be brought low. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-4-commentary
- *Christ as wisdom:* McGee says the New Testament changes the picture, because Christ has been made our wisdom and we are to love Him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-4-commentary Hippolytus says the soul embraced by wisdom becomes one with her and is filled with holiness. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0502.htm

**v. 9:** The NET notes (quoted on preceptaustin) see wedding imagery here: wisdom, like a bride, crowns her groom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-4-commentary The Pulpit Commentary's sermon notes say this crowning is really God's act, and that God's wisdom is later revealed in Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-4.html
- *Possible popular reading (vv. 8–9):* Everett's study notes say God's Word will "promote" us to the blessings of chapter 3 and that others will notice an "anointing." This sounds like popular blessing-focused teaching, but no source I read labels it as prosperity teaching. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/proverbs-4.html

**v. 10:** *Where does David's speech end?* Guzik and most commentators say verse 9. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/ The Pulpit Commentary notes that Jerome, Bede and others agree, but it thinks the father keeps speaking through verse 19. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-4.html Adam Clarke says faith, sobriety and self-control naturally lengthen life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/

**v. 11:** Waltke says the "paths" are well-worn routes that many have proved safe. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/ Henry says David taught by example and by applying general rules to particular cases. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_004.cfm

**v. 12:** Ross pictures wise living as a road without obstacles. Guzik warns parents that children trained to run in the world without God's wisdom will stumble. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/

**v. 13:** Bridges says the urgent wording shows how hard it is to hold on to our principles. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/ The Pulpit Commentary says the father knows how easily the young fall into temptation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-4.html Kitchen and the Reformation Study Bible connect this to Christ, who is called our wisdom and our life. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-4-commentary

**v. 14:** The advice is not to take even the first step onto the wicked path (Ross, citing Plaut). Clarke: never keep company with the sinful. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/ Everett's study notes say this is the path we take when we resist the Holy Spirit's leading. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/proverbs-4.html

**v. 15:** The NET notes say the rapid string of commands shows how urgent this is. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-4-commentary Henry says not to enter it even to try it out. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_004.cfm

**v. 16:** Ross calls this exaggeration for effect: the wicked are addicted to evil. Kidner notes that people can be as zealous for evil as for good. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/ Henry says doing harm is their business and their delight. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_004.cfm

**v. 17:** Sin becomes their food and drink. Trapp says the devil, their taskmaster, will not let them sleep. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/

**v. 18:** Clarke sees the sun rising to full day. Waltke says the word for "gleam" suggests not even a shadow on the path. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/ Ellicott points to Christ as the "Sun of righteousness." He says the believer's knowledge of God grows until they see Him as He is. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/4-18.htm
- *Theological emphases:* John Gill (Baptist, Calvinist) defines the "just" as those whose righteousness comes from Christ being credited to them. He says the path is Christ Himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/4-18.htm William Arnot (Scottish Presbyterian) says the sun stands for the Justifier, not the justified. https://biblehub.com/sermons/proverbs/4-18.htm Henry and Poole say growth goes on, but perfection comes only in heaven or glory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/4-18.htm Another sermon on that page defines the path simply as practising virtue. https://biblehub.com/sermons/proverbs/4-18.htm I found no Wesleyan source on this verse.

**v. 19:** Keil and Delitzsch say the wicked do not understand wickedness or the punishment it brings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/4-18.htm Henry asks what sure guide they can have once they throw God's word behind them. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-4-commentary

**v. 20:** Henry says listening carefully to God's word is a sign that grace has begun in the heart. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_004.cfm Guzik counts at least 11 body-part references in verses 20–27, showing every part of us is given either to wisdom or to evil. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/

**v. 21:** Henry: keep the words before you as your rule, and hold them as something dear that you fear losing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/4-23.html Guzik says wisdom treated as mere rules never achieves its purpose. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/

**v. 22:** Preceptaustin compares Moses calling God's word "your life" (Deuteronomy 32:47) and Jesus' words in John 5:24. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-4-commentary

**v. 23:** Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary translate it "above all that you guard." From the heart come life and death alike. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/4-23.htm Gill says the heart must be kept from vanity, error and Satan. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/proverbs/4-23.html
- *Who does the keeping?* John Flavel, a Puritan quoted on preceptaustin, says the duty is ours but the power is God's. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_423_commentary Maclaren says we must be "kept by the power of God." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/4-23.htm Guzik says the verse assumes a new heart worth keeping (Ezekiel 36:26). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/ Spurgeon says some hearts are hearts of stone and not worth keeping. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/4-23.html Preceptaustin applies the verse to controlling your thought life. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_423_commentary
- *Catholic:* catholic.com has a Q&A on this verse, but I only saw its heading and the verse text. https://www.catholic.com/qa/what-does-guard-your-heart-proverbs-423-mean

**v. 24:** Clarkson connects this to Jesus' teaching that we are justified or condemned by our words (Matthew 12:37). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-4.html

**v. 25:** I found nothing specific beyond Guzik's general point about the body parts (see v. 20).

**v. 26:** JFB reads "ponder" (KJV): a wise course comes from careful forethought. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Pro/Pro_004.cfm

**v. 27:** Guzik: never waver to the right or left from the path of the just. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-4/ Everett's study notes say verses 23–27 show God narrowing a believer's activities. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/proverbs-4.html

**Other views (whole chapter)**
- *Ancient background:* Biblehub's chapter notes compare Egyptian father-to-son teachings such as the Instruction of Amenemope. They say Proverbs is different because it roots wisdom in the fear of the LORD. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/4.htm
- *Catholic:* A catholic.com article says the Church Fathers read the book's personified wisdom as pointing to the Second Person of the Trinity. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/proverbs
- *Not found:* Orthodox readings, and any Word of Faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.
